subject: math

objective.text: Multiply a decimal by a single-digit whole number, using estimation to check the decimal point.

explanations.title: Same digits, different units
explanations.text: 31 times 4, 3.1 times 4 and 0.31 times 4 all have the digits 1, 2 and 4. The units are different, so the decimal point is in a different place.

explanations.title: Use the smallest unit
explanations.text: 5.1 is 51 tenths. 51 times 6 is 306, so the answer is 306 tenths. Estimate: 5 times 6 is 30, so the answer is 30.6.

explanations.title: Use hundredths
explanations.text: 3.12 is 312 hundredths. 312 times 4 is 1,248 hundredths. That is 12 ones 48 hundredths, or 12.48.

questions.text: Marcel rides to school and back on Tuesday and Thursday. School is 3.62 kilometers away. Exactly how many kilometers does he ride in a week?
A bake sale made $79.35. The club has 5 bake sales in all and makes the same amount each time. How much will they make after five bake sales?
Yi Ting weighs 8.3 kilograms. Her older brother is 4 times as heavy. How much does he weigh in kilograms?
Tim buys 4 gallons of white paint at $15.72 a gallon. He buys 3 gallons of blue paint at $21.87 a gallon. How much does he spend in all?
Ribbon is sold at 3 yards for $6.33. Jackie buys 24 yards. How much does she pay?
The bake sale made $79.35. Leslie says five sales will make $3,967.50. Peggy says $396.75. Use estimation to say who is right.
How can whole number multiplication help you with decimal multiplication?
Why is 306 tenths a reasonable answer for 6 times 5.1 but 306 ones is not?
Marcel can give two answers to two teachers. Why is a different answer fine for each?

hints.text: Draw the place value chart. Put each digit in its own place.
Multiplying by ten moves every digit one place to the left. Dividing moves it right.
Count the zeros in the number you multiply or divide by. That tells how many places the digits move.
The exponent tells how many tens are multiplied together. It matches the zeros.
Say the unit name. Then use a basic fact with that unit.
Think how many small units fit in a big unit. Then multiply or divide.
Add or subtract like units. Tenths with tenths, hundredths with hundredths.
Trade ten of a small unit for one of the next larger unit.
Compare digits from the left. Find the first place where they differ.
Rename both numbers with the same unit. Then compare.
Find the nearest numbers on each side for that place. Then check if you are past the halfway point.
Round the numbers and estimate first. Then place the decimal point.
Draw an area model. Multiply each unit by the whole number. Then add the partial products.
If you cannot share a unit evenly, trade it for ten of the next smaller unit.
Draw a tape diagram. Label the total and the parts.
Divide like whole numbers first. Then think about the unit to place the decimal point.
